summary: Rajkumar Sakthivel and his colleague Foss experienced a dramatic spike in their AI coding bill while working on a project with tools like Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, and CodeX. The speaker bio notes the bill jumped from £15 to £200 in a single month. Investigation revealed the core problem: these tools send excessive context—45,000 tokens per query when only about 5,000 were relevant. They tried three approaches that failed: shortening prompts (cost was already incurred before the model read the prompt), changing model settings like max tokens and temperature (affects output, not input), and output compression (worked, cutting output 75%, but output is only about 10% of cost). The key insight was that approximately 90% of AI cost is input tokens, so reducing input by 94% saves about 61% total cost versus output reduction's 8%. They built a local search layer between the codebase and AI tools with five steps: (1) AST-aware chunking with tree-sitter to break code into meaningful functions, classes, and methods; (2) parallel meaning-based vector search and keyword-based search combined; (3) result shrinking to keep only function names and descriptions; (4) relationship tracking to follow function calls across files; (5) scoring with a threshold to filter low-quality results. The dual-search approach matters because each method alone misses about 1 in 4 results, but together they miss only about 1 in 10. For scoring, they tried LLM-based judgment (too slow, added 2-3 seconds) and fixed thresholds (too simple for short questions). A simple heuristic—50% meaning score, 30% keyword score, 20% recency—worked best, running in 0.4 milliseconds with no extra AI calls. Benchmarks on FastAPI (53 files, 20 questions) showed 83K tokens per question without the tool versus 4.9K with it (94% reduction), or 523 tokens with compression, while maintaining 90% accuracy. On a real project, 247 queries saved 12.4 million tokens and £186, with 84% of savings from the search layer. Limitations include: 94% is worst-case against full file reading, real savings are lower; large mixed codebases with 396 files saw recall drop to near zero; they chose a small fast model for search over a more accurate but slower large model. The system runs locally with no data leaving the machine, provides one shared index for multiple tools, and includes memory so learned context persists across sessions. The tool, CCE, is free and open source.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Discovery
sections.summary: Raj introduces himself and his colleague Foss. They were building a project together using AI coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, CodeX) when their AI bill spiked dramatically in one month despite doing nothing different. Investigation revealed most of the cost was not the AI thinking but sending too much context—files the AI did not need, sent every time.

sections.title: The Context Problem and Failed Attempts
sections.summary: Every AI coding tool sends code as context and assumes more is better. A typical query sent 45,000 tokens but only 5,000 mattered. Three failed approaches: shortening prompts (cost already incurred before model reads prompt), changing model settings (affects output not input), and output compression (worked at 75% reduction but output is only 10% of cost). The critical insight: 90% of AI cost is input, so cutting input by 94% saves about 61% total versus 8% from output reduction.

sections.title: Local Search Layer Architecture
sections.summary: They built a local search layer between the codebase and AI. Five steps: (1) AST-aware chunking with tree-sitter breaking code into functions, classes, methods; (2) parallel meaning-based and keyword-based searches combined; (3) result shrinking to keep only function names and descriptions; (4) relationship tracking to follow function calls across files; (5) scoring with a threshold to filter low-quality results. Everything runs locally with no data leaving the machine.

sections.title: Dual Search Rationale
sections.summary: Two searches compensate for each other's weaknesses. Meaning-based search finds related ideas but misses exact names (e.g., searching for 'authenticate user' returns similar auth functions). Word-based search finds exact names but misses related ideas (e.g., searching 'login flow' misses 'sign in'). Each alone misses about 1 in 4 results; together they miss about 1 in 10.

sections.title: Scoring and Relevance Filtering
sections.summary: The hardest problem was knowing when retrieval was wrong. LLM-based scoring was too slow (2-3 seconds per query). Fixed thresholds were too simple for short questions. A simple heuristic worked best: 50% meaning score, 30% keyword score, 20% recency, with a limit adjusted based on current results. It runs in 0.4 milliseconds with no extra AI calls. Key lesson: simple formulas beat complex models most of the time.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Numbers
sections.summary: Benchmarked on FastAPI (53 files, 20 real questions): 83K tokens per question without the tool vs 4.9K with it (94% less), or 523 tokens with extra compression. Accuracy: finds the right code 90% of the time. Tests are public and reproducible.

sections.title: Limitations and Honest Trade-offs
sections.summary: The 94% figure is worst-case against reading full files every time; real tools like Claude Code are smarter, so real savings are lower. Full file baseline was used for measurement consistency. Large mixed codebases (396 files) saw recall drop almost to zero. Files that each do one thing work well; files doing many things struggle. A small fast model was chosen for search over a larger model—speed over perfection.

sections.title: Design Philosophy, Shared Index, and Memory
sections.summary: Simple choices beat complex ones: small database over big infrastructure, two searches over one fancy one, local over cloud. They built one shared index so all tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) connect to it with the same search and results. Memory was added so when one tool learns something about the project, that knowledge persists across sessions and tools—the codebase is explained once.

sections.title: Real Savings Report and Conclusion
sections.summary: Real project savings: 247 queries, 12.4 million tokens saved, nearly £186 not spent. 84% of savings came from the search layer, the rest from compression. The tool tracks every query and compares what would have been sent against what was sent, multiplied by model price. The tool is CCE, free and open source. The answer was not a better model—it was sending less. Models may account for 30% of cost but 70% is what you feed them.
